description: Comprehensive question bank derived from Cartography and Map Reading study material (3.8). Covers map fundamentals, coordinates, time calculations, scales, direction and bearings, remote sensing, GIS, GPS, projections, and Indian mapping systems.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a map?

options.B: A scaled, generalised representation of Earth's surface or another spatial area shown on a flat surface or digital display using symbols, colours, labels and a defined coordinate reference system
options.C: A collection of photographs of Earth taken from space
options.D: A written description of geographic features without any visual representation

questions.explanation: A map is a scaled, generalised representation of the whole or part of Earth's surface, or another spatial area, shown on a flat surface or digital display using symbols, colours, labels and a defined coordinate reference system.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is cartography?

options.A: The study of rocks and geological structures
options.B: The science, art and practice of designing, producing, interpreting and using maps
options.C: The measurement of land parcels for taxation

questions.explanation: Cartography is the science, art and practice of designing, producing, interpreting and using maps.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Why are maps important?

options.A: They provide entertainment through colourful designs
options.B: They communicate location, direction, distance, spatial patterns and relationships, and support navigation, land administration, planning, disaster management, resource assessment, military operations, environmental monitoring, education and decision-making
options.C: They replace the need for field surveys entirely
options.D: They are used only for historical research

questions.explanation: Maps communicate location, direction, distance, spatial patterns and relationships. They support navigation, land administration, planning, disaster management, resource assessment, military operations, environmental monitoring, education and decision-making.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which type of map shows natural features such as relief, mountains, rivers, plains and lakes?
questions.explanation: Physical maps show natural features such as relief, mountains, rivers, plains and lakes.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which type of map shows countries, states, districts, boundaries, capitals and settlements?
questions.explanation: Political maps show countries, states, districts, boundaries, capitals and settlements.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which type of map shows detailed natural and human-made features, often with contours, spot heights, roads, streams and settlements?
questions.explanation: Topographical maps show detailed natural and human-made features, often with contours, spot heights, roads, streams and settlements.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a thematic map?

options.A: A map showing only political boundaries
options.B: A map designed to show the spatial pattern of one or more related themes, such as population density, rainfall, crop production, languages or mineral distribution
options.C: A map showing individual land parcels and ownership
options.D: A map showing only natural features like rivers and mountains

questions.explanation: A thematic map is designed to show the spatial pattern of one or more related themes, such as population density, rainfall, crop production, languages or mineral distribution.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a topographical map?

options.A: A small-scale map showing only countries and continents
options.B: A detailed large- or medium-scale map that represents both natural and human-made features and commonly shows elevation using contour lines, spot heights and benchmarks
options.C: A map showing only climate data
options.D: A map used exclusively for navigation at sea

questions.explanation: A topographical map is a detailed large- or medium-scale map that represents both natural and human-made features and commonly shows elevation using contour lines, spot heights and benchmarks.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a cadastral map?

options.A: A map showing rock types and geological structures
options.B: A map showing the boundaries and identifiers of land parcels, used in land registration, revenue administration, property taxation, planning and dispute resolution
options.C: A map showing historical political boundaries

questions.explanation: A cadastral map shows the boundaries and identifiers of land parcels. It is used in land registration, revenue administration, property taxation, planning and dispute resolution.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is an atlas?

options.A: A single large-scale map of a city
options.B: A systematically organised collection of maps, often accompanied by names, indexes, tables, diagrams and explanatory text
options.C: A three-dimensional spherical model of Earth
options.D: A device used to measure atmospheric pressure

questions.explanation: An atlas is a systematically organised collection of maps, often accompanied by names, indexes, tables, diagrams and explanatory text. Atlases may be general, thematic, national, school or historical.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a globe?

options.A: A flat representation of Earth using a projection
options.B: A three-dimensional spherical model of Earth that preserves the broad geometry of the Earth more faithfully than a flat world map
options.C: A collection of maps bound in a book
options.D: A digital map displayed on a screen

questions.explanation: A globe is a three-dimensional spherical model of Earth. It preserves the broad geometry of the Earth more faithfully than a flat world map, although it is less convenient for detailed local mapping.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Why does a flat map always distort some property of Earth?

options.A: Because maps are always drawn inaccurately
options.B: Because a sphere cannot be flattened onto a plane without stretching, compressing, tearing or otherwise distorting at least one property such as area, shape, distance or direction
options.D: Because the Earth is not a perfect sphere

questions.explanation: A sphere cannot be flattened onto a plane without stretching, compressing, tearing or otherwise distorting at least one property such as area, shape, distance or direction.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are map symbols?

options.B: Conventional graphic marks used to represent real-world features, such as a line for a road or river, a point for a well or building, and an area colour for a forest or lake
options.C: Alphabetic labels used for place names
options.D: Grid lines used for coordinate reference

questions.explanation: Map symbols are conventional graphic marks used to represent real-world features, such as a line for a road or river, a point for a well or building, and an area colour for a forest or lake.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are conventional signs?

options.A: Hand-drawn sketches used by individual cartographers
options.B: Standardised symbols and patterns adopted by mapping authorities to represent features consistently
options.C: Signs used only on historical maps
options.D: Symbols that vary from map to map without any standardisation

questions.explanation: Conventional signs are standardised symbols and patterns adopted by mapping authorities to represent features consistently. Exact symbol design can vary by map series, scale and national specification.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a map legend or key?

options.A: A historical account of the map's creation
options.B: The explanatory part of a map that identifies the meaning of symbols, colours, line styles, abbreviations and patterns
options.C: A list of coordinates used on the map
options.D: A scale bar used for measuring distance

questions.explanation: A map legend or key is the explanatory part of a map that identifies the meaning of symbols, colours, line styles, abbreviations and patterns.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are the four cardinal directions?

options.D: North, South, East, West, Up, Down

questions.explanation: The four cardinal directions are North, East, South and West.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are the four intercardinal or intermediate directions?
questions.explanation: The four intercardinal or intermediate directions are Northeast, Southeast, Southwest and Northwest. The eight-point compass rose combines the four cardinal and four intercardinal directions.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are the 16-point compass directions?

options.B: The eight principal directions plus north-northeast, east-northeast, east-southeast, south-southeast, south-southwest, west-southwest, west-northwest and north-northwest
options.C: The four cardinal and four intercardinal directions only

questions.explanation: The 16-point compass directions include the eight principal directions plus north-northeast, east-northeast, east-southeast, south-southeast, south-southwest, west-southwest, west-northwest and north-northwest.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the difference between a map and a plan?

options.A: A map is always digital, while a plan is always printed
options.B: A plan usually represents a small area at a relatively large scale with considerable detail; a map may cover a much larger area and use greater generalisation
options.C: A plan shows only natural features, while a map shows only human-made features
options.D: A plan is a type of globe, while a map is flat

questions.explanation: A plan usually represents a small area at a relatively large scale with considerable detail; a map may cover a much larger area and use greater generalisation. The distinction is conventional rather than absolute.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is map generalisation?

options.A: The process of adding every possible detail to a map
options.B: The selective simplification of geographic information to suit a map's scale and purpose, which can involve omitting minor features, simplifying lines, combining objects and exaggerating important symbols
options.C: The conversion of a map from paper to digital format
options.D: The measurement of distances on a map

questions.explanation: Map generalisation is the selective simplification of geographic information to suit a map's scale and purpose. It can involve omitting minor features, simplifying lines, combining objects and exaggerating important symbols.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which type of map shows rock types, geological structures, faults, folds and age relationships?
questions.explanation: Geological maps show rock types, geological structures, faults, folds and age relationships. They are used in mineral exploration, engineering geology and earth science.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which type of map shows climate elements or classifications such as temperature, rainfall and pressure?
questions.explanation: Climatic maps show climate elements or classifications such as temperature, rainfall and pressure. They are used for climate study and regional planning.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which type of map shows past political boundaries, routes, events, settlement and territorial change?
questions.explanation: Historical maps show past political boundaries, routes, events, settlement and territorial change. They are used in historical geography and historical research.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which type of map shows the spatial occurrence or concentration of a variable, often as a thematic map?
questions.explanation: Distribution maps show the spatial occurrence or concentration of a variable, often as a thematic map. They are used for mapping population, crops, minerals or disease incidence.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which type of map represents the whole world, usually using a projection?
questions.explanation: A world map is a representation of the whole world, usually using a projection. It is used for global patterns, countries, oceans and world regions.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is latitude?

options.A: The angular distance of a point east or west of the Prime Meridian
options.B: The angular distance of a point north or south of the Equator, measured along a meridian
options.C: The height of a point above sea level

questions.explanation: Latitude is the angular distance of a point north or south of the Equator, measured along a meridian. It ranges from 0° at the Equator to 90°N or 90°S at the poles.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is longitude?

options.A: The angular distance of a point north or south of the Equator
options.B: The angular distance of a point east or west of the Prime Meridian, measured along the Equator or a parallel
options.C: The distance from the Earth's centre to its surface
options.D: The angle between true north and magnetic north

questions.explanation: Longitude is the angular distance east or west of the Prime Meridian, measured along the Equator or a parallel. It ranges from 0° to 180°E or 180°W.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the Equator?

options.A: The 0° longitude line passing through Greenwich
options.B: The 0° latitude line, an imaginary great circle equally distant from the poles, dividing Earth into the Northern and Southern Hemispheres
options.C: The line separating the Eastern and Western Hemispheres
options.D: The line where the calendar date changes

questions.explanation: The Equator is the 0° latitude line, an imaginary great circle equally distant from the poles. It divides Earth into the Northern and Southern Hemispheres.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the Prime Meridian?

options.B: The 0° longitude line adopted by international convention, dividing the Eastern and Western Hemispheres
options.D: The line passing through the Tropic of Cancer

questions.explanation: The Prime Meridian is the 0° longitude line adopted by international convention. It divides the Eastern and Western Hemispheres.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a parallel of latitude?

options.A: A semicircle joining the North and South Poles
options.B: A circle on Earth's surface joining points of equal latitude; parallels are parallel to the Equator, and the Equator is the only great circle among them

questions.explanation: A parallel of latitude is a circle on Earth's surface joining points of equal latitude. Parallels are parallel to the Equator; the Equator is the only great circle among them.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a meridian?

options.A: A circle parallel to the Equator
options.B: A semicircle joining the North and South Poles; opposite meridians together form a great circle
options.D: A line indicating the direction of magnetic north

questions.explanation: A meridian is a semicircle joining the North and South Poles. Opposite meridians together form a great circle.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are the important meridians mentioned in the text?

options.A: The Equator, Tropic of Cancer, Tropic of Capricorn
options.B: The Prime Meridian at 0°, the 180° meridian, and meridians used as national standard-time references, such as 82°30′E for Indian Standard Time
options.C: The Arctic Circle and Antarctic Circle

questions.explanation: The important meridians are the Prime Meridian at 0°, the 180° meridian, and meridians used as national standard-time references, such as 82°30′E for Indian Standard Time.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the International Date Line (IDL)?

options.A: A line that exactly follows the 180° meridian
options.B: A conventional line, mostly following 180° longitude through the Pacific, where the calendar date changes by one day when crossed; it bends around countries and island groups to avoid splitting them
options.C: The 0° longitude line passing through Greenwich
options.D: The line separating the Northern and Southern Hemispheres

questions.explanation: The International Date Line is a conventional line, mostly following 180° longitude through the Pacific, where the calendar date changes by one day when crossed. It bends around countries and island groups to avoid splitting them.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Does the International Date Line exactly follow 180° longitude?

options.B: No, it deviates substantially to accommodate political boundaries and island groups; the 180° meridian is a useful geographic reference but not the exact practical IDL
options.C: Yes, but only in the Northern Hemisphere
options.D: No, it follows the Prime Meridian instead

questions.explanation: No, the IDL deviates substantially to accommodate political boundaries and island groups. The 180° meridian is a useful geographic reference but not the exact practical IDL.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are geographical coordinates?

options.A: A location reference usually expressed as latitude and longitude, sometimes with elevation and a specified datum; latitude is written first, followed by longitude
options.B: A location reference expressed only as longitude and latitude in any order
options.C: A grid reference using eastings and northings only
options.D: A measurement of distance between two points

questions.explanation: Geographical coordinates are a location reference usually expressed as latitude and longitude, sometimes with elevation and a specified datum. Latitude is written first, followed by longitude.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is angular distance?

options.A: The straight-line distance between two points on the ground
options.B: The angle between a point's position and a reference line or plane, expressed in degrees, minutes and seconds or decimal degrees
options.C: The height of a point above sea level
options.D: The difference between local time and standard time

questions.explanation: Angular distance is the angle between a point's position and a reference line or plane, expressed in degrees, minutes and seconds or decimal degrees.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: How are degrees, minutes and seconds related?

options.A: One degree equals 100 minutes; one minute equals 100 seconds
options.B: One degree equals 60 minutes; one minute equals 60 seconds; thus 1° = 60′ = 3,600″
options.C: One degree equals 60 seconds; one minute equals 60 degrees
options.D: One degree equals 360 minutes; one minute equals 60 seconds

questions.explanation: One degree equals 60 minutes; one minute equals 60 seconds. Thus 1° = 60′ = 3,600″.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: How much time difference corresponds to 1° of longitude?

options.A: One minute of mean solar time
options.B: Four minutes of mean solar time
options.C: Fifteen minutes of mean solar time
options.D: One hour of mean solar time

questions.explanation: Four minutes of mean solar time, because Earth rotates 360° in approximately 24 hours: 24 hours ÷ 360° = 4 minutes per degree.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: How is local mean solar time estimated from longitude?

options.A: By adding longitude degrees to standard time
options.B: Compared with Greenwich mean solar time, local mean solar time is later to the east and earlier to the west; time difference = longitude difference × 4 minutes per degree
options.C: By dividing longitude by 15 and adding 1 hour

questions.explanation: Compared with Greenwich mean solar time, local mean solar time is later to the east and earlier to the west. Time difference = longitude difference × 4 minutes per degree.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: A place is at 75°E and Greenwich is at 0°. What is the local mean solar-time difference?
questions.explanation: 75 × 4 = 300 minutes = 5 hours. The place at 75°E is five hours ahead of Greenwich mean solar time.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: If it is 12:00 noon at Greenwich, what is the local mean solar time at 90°E?
questions.explanation: 90 × 4 = 360 minutes = 6 hours. It is 18:00 (6:00 p.m.) at 90°E.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: If it is 12:00 noon at Greenwich, what is the local mean solar time at 30°W?
questions.explanation: 30 × 4 = 120 minutes = 2 hours. It is 10:00 a.m. at 30°W.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What happens to the calendar date when the International Date Line is crossed eastward?

options.A: The date is moved back by one day
options.B: The date is advanced by one day
options.D: The date changes by one month

questions.explanation: When crossing the IDL eastward, the calendar date is advanced by one day. For example, Thursday becomes Friday, subject to local convention and time-zone arrangement.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What happens when the International Date Line is crossed westward?

options.A: The calendar date is advanced by one day
options.B: The calendar date is moved back by one day
options.D: The calendar date changes by one year

questions.explanation: When crossing the IDL westward, the calendar date is moved back by one day. For example, Friday becomes Thursday.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is Greenwich Mean Time (GMT)?

options.A: The modern international civil-time standard based on atomic time
options.B: Originally the mean solar time at the Greenwich meridian; it remains widely used as a time reference in everyday language, but UTC is the modern international civil-time standard
options.D: A time zone used only in the Pacific Ocean

questions.explanation: GMT originally referred to mean solar time at the Greenwich meridian. It remains widely used as a time reference in everyday language, but UTC is the modern international civil-time standard.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is Coordinated Universal Time (UTC)?

options.A: A time standard based on the Sun's position at Greenwich
options.B: The internationally coordinated time standard based on atomic time, with leap-second adjustments historically used to keep it close to Earth's irregular rotation; it is the basis for civil time-zone offsets
options.C: The standard time of the International Date Line
options.D: A local solar time used only in Europe

questions.explanation: UTC is the internationally coordinated time standard based on atomic time, with leap-second adjustments historically used to keep it close to Earth's irregular rotation. It is the basis for civil time-zone offsets.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is Indian Standard Time (IST)?

options.C: UTC+5:30, based on the 82°30′E standard meridian passing near Mirzapur in Uttar Pradesh

questions.explanation: IST is UTC+5:30, based on the 82°30′E standard meridian passing near Mirzapur in Uttar Pradesh. It is used throughout India.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Why does India use one standard time despite its large east-west extent?

options.A: Because India has no east-west extent
options.B: A single national time standard simplifies administration, transport, communication and commerce; local solar time still differs across the country
options.C: Because the Sun rises at the same time everywhere in India

questions.explanation: A single national time standard simplifies administration, transport, communication and commerce. Local solar time still differs across the country.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: How much local solar-time difference is there between India's approximate eastern and western longitudes?
questions.explanation: India spans roughly 68°7′E to 97°25′E, a longitude difference of about 29°18′. At four minutes per degree, the local solar-time difference is approximately 1 hour 57 minutes.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a time zone?

options.A: A region that uses the same standard civil time, usually defined as an offset from UTC, with boundaries that follow political and administrative decisions rather than exact meridians
options.B: A region where local solar time is exactly the same everywhere
options.C: A line of longitude where the date changes
options.D: A region that uses only GMT

questions.explanation: A time zone is a region that uses the same standard civil time, usually defined as an offset from UTC. Actual boundaries follow political and administrative decisions rather than exact meridians.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the difference between local solar time and standard time?

options.A: Local solar time is based on the Sun's apparent position at a longitude; standard time is the legally adopted clock time for a region or country, often shared across a broad area
options.B: Local solar time is legally adopted; standard time is based on the Sun's position
options.C: There is no difference between them
options.D: Local solar time is used only at sea; standard time is used only on land

questions.explanation: Local solar time is based on the Sun's apparent position at a longitude. Standard time is the legally adopted clock time for a region or country, often shared across a broad area.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the difference between GMT and UTC in modern timekeeping?

options.A: They are exactly identical in technical definition
options.B: UTC is the precise international standard; GMT is a historical mean-solar-time reference and is often used informally as equivalent to UTC for civil-time purposes, but they are not identical in technical definition
options.C: GMT is based on atomic time; UTC is based on solar time
options.D: GMT is used only in India; UTC is used only in Europe

questions.explanation: UTC is the precise international standard. GMT is a historical mean-solar-time reference and is often used informally as equivalent to UTC for civil-time purposes, but they are not identical in technical definition.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: At 60°E, when it is 08:00 at 0° longitude, what is the local time?
questions.explanation: 60 × 4 = 240 minutes = 4 hours; east is ahead. 08:00 + 4 hours = 12:00 noon.
questions.source: Cartography and Map Reading, Section 3.8.2 (Worked examples)

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: At 45°W, when it is 15:00 at Greenwich, what is the local time?
questions.explanation: 45 × 4 = 180 minutes = 3 hours; west is behind. 15:00 − 3 hours = 12:00 noon.
questions.source: Cartography and Map Reading, Section 3.8.2 (Worked examples)

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Two places differ by 7°30′ longitude. What is the solar-time difference?
questions.explanation: 7.5 × 4 = 30 minutes.
questions.source: Cartography and Map Reading, Section 3.8.2 (Worked examples)

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: If local time at 90°E is 18:00, what is it at 30°E?
questions.explanation: Difference = 60° × 4 = 240 minutes = 4 hours; 30°E is west of 90°E, so 18:00 − 4 hours = 14:00 (2:00 p.m.).
questions.source: Cartography and Map Reading, Section 3.8.2 (Worked examples)

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: A traveller crosses the IDL westward on Sunday. What day is it after crossing?
questions.explanation: Westward crossing advances the date by one day, subject to local clock-time conventions in view.
questions.source: Cartography and Map Reading, Section 3.8.2 (Worked examples)

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the latitude of the Tropic of Cancer?
questions.explanation: The Tropic of Cancer is approximately 23°26′ N. It is the northern limit of overhead Sun during the year and passes through India.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the latitude of the Tropic of Capricorn?
questions.explanation: The Tropic of Capricorn is approximately 23°26′ S. It is the southern limit of overhead Sun during the year.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the latitude of the Arctic Circle?
questions.explanation: The Arctic Circle is approximately 66°34′ N. It is the boundary of the region experiencing at least one 24-hour day or night each year.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the latitude of the Antarctic Circle?
questions.explanation: The Antarctic Circle is approximately 66°34′ S. It is the southern counterpart of the Arctic Circle.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is map scale?

options.A: The relationship between a distance measured on a map and the corresponding horizontal distance on the ground
options.B: The size of the paper on which a map is printed
options.C: The number of symbols used on a map
options.D: The height of the map above sea level

questions.explanation: Map scale is the relationship between a distance measured on a map and the corresponding horizontal distance on the ground.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a statement scale?

options.A: A scale expressed as a unitless ratio
options.B: A scale expressed in words, such as '1 centimetre represents 1 kilometre'
options.C: A drawn line or bar divided into labelled ground-distance intervals
options.D: A scale based on the representative fraction

questions.explanation: A statement scale is a scale expressed in words, such as '1 centimetre represents 1 kilometre'.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a representative fraction (RF)?

options.B: A unitless ratio of map distance to ground distance expressed in the same units; for example, 1:50,000 means one unit on the map represents 50,000 of the same units on the ground
options.C: A drawn line or bar divided into labelled ground-distance intervals
options.D: The ratio between a distance on a projection and the corresponding distance on the reference surface

questions.explanation: A representative fraction is a unitless ratio of map distance to ground distance expressed in the same units. For example, 1:50,000 means one unit on the map represents 50,000 of the same units on the ground.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a linear or graphic scale?

options.B: A unitless ratio of map distance to ground distance
options.C: A drawn line or bar divided into labelled ground-distance intervals; it remains usable after proportional enlargement or reduction of the map, provided the bar is resized with the map
options.D: The ratio between a distance on a projection and the corresponding distance on the reference surface

questions.explanation: A linear or graphic scale is a drawn line or bar divided into labelled ground-distance intervals. It remains usable after proportional enlargement or reduction of the map, provided the bar is resized with the map.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a large-scale map?

options.A: A map with a relatively large representative fraction, such as 1:5,000 or 1:25,000; it covers a smaller area and shows more detail
options.B: A map with a relatively small representative fraction, such as 1:1,000,000; it covers a larger area and shows less detail
options.C: A map printed on large paper
options.D: A map that covers the whole world

questions.explanation: A large-scale map has a relatively large representative fraction, such as 1:5,000 or 1:25,000. It covers a smaller area and shows more detail.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a small-scale map?

options.A: A map with a relatively large representative fraction, such as 1:5,000
options.B: A map with a relatively small representative fraction, such as 1:1,000,000; it covers a larger area and shows less detail
options.C: A map printed on small paper
options.D: A map that covers only a small area

questions.explanation: A small-scale map has a relatively small representative fraction, such as 1:1,000,000. It covers a larger area and shows less detail.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which is larger scale: 1:10,000 or 1:100,000?
questions.explanation: 1:10,000 is the larger scale because a map unit represents fewer ground units and therefore more detail can be shown.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: How is ground distance calculated from a representative fraction?

options.A: Ground distance = map distance ÷ scale denominator
options.B: Ground distance = map distance × scale denominator, after converting both to the same units
options.C: Ground distance = map distance + scale denominator
options.D: Ground distance = scale denominator ÷ map distance

questions.explanation: Ground distance = map distance × scale denominator, after converting both to the same units.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: A map has RF 1:50,000. What ground distance does 4 cm represent?

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: On a map, 5 cm represents 10 km. What is the RF?

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: A road is 12 km long. How long will it be on a 1:250,000 map?

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Why must units be converted before using RF?

options.A: Because the numerator and denominator of an RF must be expressed in the same units; otherwise the ratio is invalid
options.B: Because RF requires units to be in kilometres only
options.C: Because RF is always expressed in centimetres
options.D: Because conversion changes the scale of the map

questions.explanation: The numerator and denominator of an RF must be expressed in the same units; otherwise the ratio is invalid.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the difference between map scale and map resolution?

options.A: Scale describes the ratio between map and ground distances; resolution describes the smallest detail that can be distinguished, often in relation to pixel size or positional precision in digital data
options.B: Scale describes pixel size; resolution describes ground distance
options.D: Scale applies only to digital maps; resolution applies only to paper maps

questions.explanation: Scale describes the ratio between map and ground distances. Resolution describes the smallest detail that can be distinguished, often in relation to pixel size or positional precision in digital data.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a verbal or statement scale's limitation?

options.A: It cannot be used on topographic maps
options.B: It becomes incorrect if a map is enlarged or reduced without changing the written statement; a graphic bar scale changes proportionally with the map
options.C: It requires conversion to a representative fraction before use
options.D: It is only valid for small-scale maps

questions.explanation: A verbal or statement scale becomes incorrect if a map is enlarged or reduced without changing the written statement. A graphic bar scale changes proportionally with the map.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is scale factor in a map projection?

options.A: The ratio between a distance on the projection and the corresponding distance on the reference surface; it varies by location and direction in many projections, reflecting projection distortion
options.B: The ratio between map distance and ground distance
options.C: The size of the map sheet
options.D: The number of grid lines per centimetre

questions.explanation: Scale factor in a map projection is the ratio between a distance on the projection and the corresponding distance on the reference surface. It varies by location and direction in many projections, reflecting projection distortion.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a compass?

options.A: A direction-finding instrument that indicates direction relative to a reference, traditionally using a magnetised needle aligned approximately with Earth's magnetic field
options.B: A device used to measure atmospheric pressure
options.C: An instrument used to measure ground distance
options.D: A tool used to draw circles on maps

questions.explanation: A compass is a direction-finding instrument that indicates direction relative to a reference, traditionally using a magnetised needle aligned approximately with Earth's magnetic field.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a magnetic compass?

options.A: A compass whose magnetised needle aligns with the horizontal component of Earth's magnetic field and points toward magnetic north, not necessarily geographic true north
options.B: A compass that always points to the geographic North Pole
options.C: A compass that uses GPS signals to determine direction
options.D: A compass that measures distance rather than direction

questions.explanation: A magnetic compass is a compass whose magnetised needle aligns with the horizontal component of Earth's magnetic field. It points toward magnetic north, not necessarily geographic true north.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is true north?

options.A: The direction indicated by a magnetic compass needle
options.B: The direction along a meridian toward the geographic North Pole
options.C: The direction of grid lines on a map

questions.explanation: True north is the direction along a meridian toward the geographic North Pole.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is magnetic declination?

options.A: The angle between true north and magnetic north at a particular place and time; it varies geographically and changes over time
options.B: The angle between the Equator and a meridian
options.C: The difference between local solar time and standard time
options.D: The angle between grid north and true north

questions.explanation: Magnetic declination is the angle between true north and magnetic north at a particular place and time. It varies geographically and changes over time.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a bearing?

options.A: A horizontal direction expressed as an angle measured clockwise from a reference direction, commonly true north or grid north; in whole-circle bearings it ranges from 000° to 360°
options.B: The vertical angle of a slope
options.C: The distance between two points on a map

questions.explanation: A bearing is a horizontal direction expressed as an angle measured clockwise from a reference direction, commonly true north or grid north. In whole-circle bearings it ranges from 000° to 360°.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a back bearing?

options.A: The direction exactly opposite to a given bearing; for a whole-circle bearing, add 180° if the original is less than 180° or subtract 180° if it is 180° or more
options.B: The bearing measured from magnetic north instead of true north
options.C: The bearing measured in a counter-clockwise direction
options.D: The bearing of the previous measurement

questions.explanation: A back bearing is the direction exactly opposite to a given bearing. For a whole-circle bearing, add 180° if the original is less than 180° or subtract 180° if it is 180° or more.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the bearing of east, south and west in whole-circle notation from north?
questions.explanation: In whole-circle notation from north, East = 090°, South = 180° and West = 270°.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is relative location?

options.A: A precise position expressed using coordinates or an address
options.B: The position of a place described in relation to another place or feature, such as 'north of Bengaluru' or 'west of the river'
options.C: The location of a place on a grid using eastings and northings
options.D: The location of a place determined by GPS

questions.explanation: Relative location is the position of a place described in relation to another place or feature, such as 'north of Bengaluru' or 'west of the river'.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is absolute location?

options.A: A position described relative to another place
options.B: A precise position expressed using coordinates, an address, a parcel identifier or another fixed reference system
options.C: A location determined only by a compass bearing
options.D: A location that changes over time

questions.explanation: Absolute location is a precise position expressed using coordinates, an address, a parcel identifier or another fixed reference system.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a grid reference?

options.A: A method of identifying a location within a map grid using letters, numbers or coordinate values; in standard map-reading practice, eastings are read before northings
options.B: A reference to the map legend
options.C: A reference to the map scale
options.D: A reference to the compass rose

questions.explanation: A grid reference is a method of identifying a location within a map grid using letters, numbers or coordinate values. In standard map-reading practice, eastings are read before northings.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What does 'eastings before northings' mean?

options.A: When giving a grid reference, state the vertical grid value first, then the horizontal grid value
options.B: When giving a grid reference, state the horizontal grid value (easting) first, then the vertical grid value (northing), following the rule 'along the corridor, then up the stairs'
options.C: When giving a grid reference, state latitude first, then longitude
options.D: When giving a grid reference, state the map scale first, then the coordinates

questions.explanation: When giving a grid reference, state the horizontal grid value (easting) first, then the vertical grid value (northing), following the rule 'along the corridor, then up the stairs'.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a four-figure grid reference?

options.A: A reference identifying a 1 km grid square on many standard topographic maps, using the easting and northing values of the square's southwest corner; actual grid interval depends on the map series
options.B: A reference locating a point to about 100 m precision
options.C: A reference using latitude and longitude
options.D: A reference using a compass bearing and distance

questions.explanation: A four-figure grid reference identifies a 1 km grid square on many standard topographic maps, using the easting and northing values of the square's southwest corner. Actual grid interval depends on the map series.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a six-figure grid reference?

options.A: A reference identifying a 1 km grid square
options.B: A more precise reference locating a point within a grid square, commonly to about 100 m on a 1 km grid when the map scale and grid support that precision
options.C: A reference using latitude and longitude to six decimal places
options.D: A reference identifying a 10 km grid square

questions.explanation: A six-figure grid reference is a more precise reference locating a point within a grid square, commonly to about 100 m on a 1 km grid when the map scale and grid support that precision.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: How should coordinates be written?

options.A: Longitude first, then latitude; specify E or W and N or S
options.B: Write latitude first, then longitude; specify N or S and E or W, or use signed decimal degrees with a stated convention; for example, 12.97°N 77.59°E
options.C: Write elevation first, then latitude and longitude
options.D: Write grid reference first, then latitude and longitude

questions.explanation: Write latitude first, then longitude; specify N or S and E or W, or use signed decimal degrees with a stated convention. For example, 12.97°N 77.59°E.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: How do you identify a location from coordinates?

options.A: Locate the latitude parallel and longitude meridian, then find their intersection; on a digital map or GIS, enter the coordinates using the correct datum and coordinate format
options.B: Measure the distance from the map corner
options.C: Use a compass bearing from a known landmark
options.D: Read the grid reference from the map legend

questions.explanation: To identify a location from coordinates, locate the latitude parallel and longitude meridian, then find their intersection. On a digital map or GIS, enter the coordinates using the correct datum and coordinate format.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a compass rose?

options.A: A map symbol showing north and often other cardinal or intermediate directions
options.C: A symbol used to indicate elevation
options.D: A device used to measure magnetic declination

questions.explanation: A compass rose is a map symbol showing north and often other cardinal or intermediate directions.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Why can a compass bearing differ from a map-grid bearing?

options.A: Because a map grid may be aligned to grid north, while a compass points to magnetic north and geographic meridians indicate true north; grid convergence and magnetic declination create differences
options.C: Because map grids are always aligned to magnetic north
options.D: Because bearings are measured counter-clockwise on a map

questions.explanation: A map grid may be aligned to grid north, while a compass points to magnetic north and geographic meridians indicate true north. Grid convergence and magnetic declination create differences.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is remote sensing?

options.A: The acquisition of information about Earth's surface or atmosphere without direct physical contact, typically using sensors on satellites, aircraft, drones or other platforms
options.B: The measurement of distances on a map using a scale
options.C: The determination of position using GPS
options.D: The analysis of spatial data in a GIS

questions.explanation: Remote sensing is the acquisition of information about Earth's surface or atmosphere without direct physical contact, typically using sensors on satellites, aircraft, drones or other platforms.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are the main components of a remote-sensing system?

options.A: An energy source or illumination; interaction with the atmosphere and target; a sensor on a platform; data transmission and processing; interpretation; and ground truth or validation
options.B: A map, a scale, a legend and a compass rose
options.C: A GPS receiver, a computer and a printer
options.D: A satellite, a ground station and a user

questions.explanation: The main components of a remote-sensing system are an energy source or illumination; interaction with the atmosphere and target; a sensor on a platform; data transmission and processing; interpretation; and ground truth or validation.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the difference between passive and active remote sensing?

options.A: Passive sensors emit their own energy; active sensors detect naturally available energy
options.B: Passive sensors detect naturally available energy, such as reflected sunlight or emitted thermal radiation; active sensors emit their own energy and measure the return, as in radar and lidar
options.C: Passive sensors work only at night; active sensors work only during the day
options.D: Passive sensors are used only on satellites; active sensors are used only on aircraft

questions.explanation: Passive sensors detect naturally available energy, such as reflected sunlight or emitted thermal radiation. Active sensors emit their own energy and measure the return, as in radar and lidar.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is aerial photography?

options.A: The capture of photographs of Earth's surface from aircraft, drones or other airborne platforms; used in surveying, mapping, land-use studies, infrastructure planning and disaster assessment
options.B: The capture of photographs from satellites only
options.C: The capture of photographs from the ground
options.D: The analysis of photographs in a GIS

questions.explanation: Aerial photography is the capture of photographs of Earth's surface from aircraft, drones or other airborne platforms. It is used in surveying, mapping, land-use studies, infrastructure planning and disaster assessment.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is satellite imagery?

options.B: Digital or photographic data collected by sensors carried on satellites; it can provide repeated, large-area observations for land, ocean, atmosphere, agriculture, forestry, water and disaster monitoring
options.D: Data collected by ground-based sensors only

questions.explanation: Satellite imagery is digital or photographic data collected by sensors carried on satellites. It can provide repeated, large-area observations for land, ocean, atmosphere, agriculture, forestry, water and disaster monitoring.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are spatial, spectral, radiometric and temporal resolutions?

options.A: Spatial resolution describes ground detail or pixel size; spectral resolution describes the number and width of wavelength bands; radiometric resolution describes sensitivity to differences in energy; temporal resolution describes how frequently a sensor revisits or acquires the same area
options.B: Spatial resolution describes the number of bands; spectral resolution describes pixel size; radiometric resolution describes revisit time; temporal resolution describes energy sensitivity
options.C: All four terms refer to the same concept
options.D: Spatial resolution describes time; spectral resolution describes distance; radiometric resolution describes colour; temporal resolution describes position

questions.explanation: Spatial resolution describes ground detail or pixel size; spectral resolution describes the number and width of wavelength bands; radiometric resolution describes sensitivity to differences in energy; temporal resolution describes how frequently a sensor revisits or acquires the same area.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is ground truth in remote sensing?

options.A: Field observations or measurements used to verify and calibrate the interpretation of remotely sensed data
options.B: The elevation of the ground above sea level
options.C: The true north direction on a map
options.D: The base map used in a GIS

questions.explanation: Ground truth in remote sensing refers to field observations or measurements used to verify and calibrate the interpretation of remotely sensed data.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is GIS?

options.B: A Geographic Information System: an organised framework of hardware, software, data, people and methods for capturing, storing, managing, analysing and displaying geographically referenced information

questions.explanation: GIS is a Geographic Information System: an organised framework of hardware, software, data, people and methods for capturing, storing, managing, analysing and displaying geographically referenced information.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are the main data models in GIS?

options.A: Raster data represent space as a grid of cells or pixels; vector data represent discrete features as points, lines and polygons; attribute tables store descriptive information linked to spatial features
options.B: Raster data represent features as points and lines; vector data represent space as a grid of cells
options.C: Only one data model exists in GIS
options.D: GIS uses only tables, not spatial data

questions.explanation: Raster data represent space as a grid of cells or pixels; vector data represent discrete features as points, lines and polygons. Attribute tables store descriptive information linked to spatial features.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are common GIS operations?

options.A: Overlay, buffering, spatial query, network analysis, interpolation, terrain analysis, geocoding, proximity analysis, map algebra and spatial statistics

questions.explanation: Common GIS operations include overlay, buffering, spatial query, network analysis, interpolation, terrain analysis, geocoding, proximity analysis, map algebra and spatial statistics.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is GPS?

options.B: The Global Positioning System: the United States-operated satellite-based radio-navigation system that provides positioning, navigation and timing services worldwide

questions.explanation: GPS is the Global Positioning System, the United States-operated satellite-based radio-navigation system that provides positioning, navigation and timing services worldwide.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is GNSS?

options.A: Global Navigation Satellite System: the general term for satellite navigation constellations; GPS is one GNSS, and others include India's NavIC, Russia's GLONASS, Europe's Galileo and China's BeiDou

questions.explanation: GNSS stands for Global Navigation Satellite System, the general term for satellite navigation constellations. GPS is one GNSS; others include India's NavIC, Russia's GLONASS, Europe's Galileo and China's BeiDou.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: How does satellite navigation determine a position?

options.A: A receiver measures signal travel times from multiple satellites and uses trilateration with satellite clock and orbit information; at least four satellites are normally used to solve for three-dimensional position and receiver-clock offset
options.B: A receiver measures the distance to a single satellite
options.C: A receiver uses a compass and a map
options.D: A receiver uses satellite imagery and image processing

questions.explanation: A receiver measures signal travel times from multiple satellites and uses trilateration with satellite clock and orbit information. At least four satellites are normally used to solve for three-dimensional position and receiver-clock offset.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the difference between GPS and GIS?

options.A: GPS/GNSS determines a receiver's position and time; GIS stores, integrates, analyses and visualises spatial data; GPS can provide data that are then used in GIS
options.B: GPS stores and analyses spatial data; GIS determines position
options.D: GPS is used only for mapping; GIS is used only for navigation

questions.explanation: GPS/GNSS determines a receiver's position and time. GIS stores, integrates, analyses and visualises spatial data. GPS can provide data that are then used in GIS.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is digital mapping?

options.A: The creation, storage, analysis and display of maps in digital form, including web maps, mobile maps, navigation maps and GIS-based products
options.B: The scanning of paper maps only
options.C: The use of a compass and paper map
options.D: The printing of maps on a digital printer

questions.explanation: Digital mapping is the creation, storage, analysis and display of maps in digital form, including web maps, mobile maps, navigation maps and GIS-based products.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a cartographic projection?

options.A: A systematic mathematical transformation of geographic coordinates on Earth's curved reference surface to a flat map plane
options.B: A method of measuring distances on a map
options.D: A way of determining magnetic declination

questions.explanation: A cartographic projection is a systematic mathematical transformation of geographic coordinates on Earth's curved reference surface to a flat map plane.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Why are map projections necessary?

options.A: Because a flat sheet or screen cannot represent the curved Earth without distortion; projections make it possible to display, measure and analyse spatial information on a plane
options.B: Because maps are always drawn on paper
options.D: Because projections are required by international law

questions.explanation: A flat sheet or screen cannot represent the curved Earth without distortion. Projections make it possible to display, measure and analyse spatial information on a plane.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are the properties and limitations of the Mercator projection?

options.A: Conformal; preserves local angles and shapes; useful for marine navigation and rhumb lines; area distortion increases strongly toward the poles, making Greenland appear disproportionately large
options.B: Equal-area; preserves area but distorts shape
options.C: Azimuthal; preserves distances from the centre

questions.explanation: The Mercator projection is conformal, preserving local angles and shapes, and is useful for marine navigation and rhumb lines. Area distortion increases strongly toward the poles; Greenland appears disproportionately large.
questions.source: Cartography and Map Reading, Section 3.8.5 (Projection table)

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are the properties and limitations of the Transverse Mercator projection?

options.A: Conformal cylindrical projection oriented across a central meridian; used by UTM zones; distortion grows away from the central meridian, and the world is divided into zones
options.B: Equal-area projection used for world maps
options.C: Azimuthal projection used for polar regions
options.D: Conic projection used for mid-latitude regions

questions.explanation: Transverse Mercator is a conformal cylindrical projection oriented across a central meridian, used by UTM zones. Distortion grows away from the central meridian; the world is divided into zones.
questions.source: Cartography and Map Reading, Section 3.8.5 (Projection table)

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the Universal Transverse Mercator (UTM) grid?

options.A: A global projected coordinate system divided into 60 longitudinal zones, each 6° wide, using Transverse Mercator projection; UTM coordinates are expressed as eastings and northings in metres
options.B: A grid system using latitude and longitude only
options.C: A grid system used only in the United States
options.D: A grid system based on the Mercator projection

questions.explanation: The UTM grid is a global projected coordinate system divided into 60 longitudinal zones, each 6° wide, using Transverse Mercator projection. UTM coordinates are expressed as eastings and northings in metres.
questions.source: Cartography and Map Reading, Section 3.8.5 (Projection table)

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are the properties and limitations of the Lambert Conformal Conic projection?

options.A: Conformal conic projection suited to mid-latitude regions with east-west extent; area and distance are not generally preserved everywhere
options.B: Equal-area projection used for world maps
options.D: Azimuthal projection used for polar regions

questions.explanation: Lambert Conformal Conic is a conformal conic projection suited to mid-latitude regions with east-west extent. Area and distance are not generally preserved everywhere.
questions.source: Cartography and Map Reading, Section 3.8.5 (Projection table)

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are the properties and limitations of the Albers Equal-Area Conic projection?

options.A: Preserves area; useful for thematic maps of continental or regional areas; shapes and angles may be distorted
options.B: Preserves shape and angles; useful for navigation

questions.explanation: Albers Equal-Area Conic preserves area and is useful for thematic maps of continental or regional areas. Shapes and angles may be distorted.
questions.source: Cartography and Map Reading, Section 3.8.5 (Projection table)

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are the properties and limitations of the Azimuthal equidistant projection?

options.A: Distances and directions from the centre are represented correctly; distortion increases away from the centre, and not all pairwise distances are preserved
options.D: Is a compromise projection for world maps

questions.explanation: Azimuthal equidistant represents distances and directions from the centre correctly. Distortion increases away from the centre; not all pairwise distances are preserved.
questions.source: Cartography and Map Reading, Section 3.8.5 (Projection table)

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are the properties and limitations of the Robinson projection?

options.A: Compromise world projection designed for balanced visual appearance; neither conformal nor equal-area, and several properties are distorted
options.C: Equal-area projection used for thematic maps
options.D: Azimuthal projection used for polar regions

questions.explanation: Robinson is a compromise world projection designed for balanced visual appearance. It is neither conformal nor equal-area, and several properties are distorted.
questions.source: Cartography and Map Reading, Section 3.8.5 (Projection table)

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What does a conformal projection preserve?

options.B: Local angles and shapes at sufficiently small scales, not area or all distances; Mercator is the classic conformal projection
options.C: All distances between all pairs of points

questions.explanation: A conformal projection preserves local angles and shapes at sufficiently small scales, not area or all distances. Mercator is the classic conformal projection.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What does an equal-area projection preserve?

options.B: Area relationships: regions retain their correct relative areas, although shape, angle and distance may be distorted

questions.explanation: An equal-area projection preserves area relationships: regions retain their correct relative areas, although shape, angle and distance may be distorted.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What does an equidistant projection preserve?

options.C: Distances from one or more specified points or along selected lines, depending on the projection; it does not preserve every distance between every pair of points

questions.explanation: An equidistant projection preserves distances from one or more specified points or along selected lines, depending on the projection. It does not preserve every distance between every pair of points.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is map distortion?

options.A: The unavoidable alteration of area, shape, distance or direction when a curved surface is represented on a plane; the nature and amount of distortion depend on the projection and location
options.B: An error made by the mapmaker
options.C: A problem that can be completely eliminated by any projection
options.D: The difference between map scale and ground distance

questions.explanation: Map distortion is the unavoidable alteration of area, shape, distance or direction when a curved surface is represented on a plane. The nature and amount of distortion depend on the projection and location.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a datum?

options.A: A reference framework defining the size and shape of Earth and the origin, orientation and scale of a coordinate system; coordinates can differ when expressed on different datums
options.B: A line of latitude or longitude
options.D: A unit of distance used on maps

questions.explanation: A datum is a reference framework defining the size and shape of Earth and the origin, orientation and scale of a coordinate system. Coordinates can differ when expressed on different datums.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is WGS 84?

options.A: A map projection used for world maps
options.B: World Geodetic System 1984, a widely used global geodetic reference system associated with GPS and many digital mapping applications
options.C: A satellite navigation system developed by India

questions.explanation: WGS 84 is the World Geodetic System 1984, a widely used global geodetic reference system associated with GPS and many digital mapping applications.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is georeferencing?

options.A: Assigning real-world coordinates to a map, image or dataset so it can be correctly positioned and integrated with other spatial data
options.D: Projecting a map onto a flat surface

questions.explanation: Georeferencing is assigning real-world coordinates to a map, image or dataset so it can be correctly positioned and integrated with other spatial data.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is geocoding?

options.A: Assigning coordinates to a map image
options.B: Converting a textual location description, such as an address or place name, into geographic coordinates
options.D: Projecting a map onto a flat surface

questions.explanation: Geocoding is converting a textual location description, such as an address or place name, into geographic coordinates.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a digital elevation model (DEM)?

options.A: A digital representation of terrain elevation; DEMs support slope, aspect, watershed, visibility, contour and terrain modelling analyses
options.B: A digital map showing political boundaries
options.C: A digital model of Earth's magnetic field
options.D: A digital model of the atmosphere

questions.explanation: A digital elevation model (DEM) is a digital representation of terrain elevation. DEMs support slope, aspect, watershed, visibility, contour and terrain modelling analyses.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the Survey of India?

options.A: An ISRO centre responsible for remote-sensing data
options.B: Survey of India (SoI), under the Department of Science and Technology, is India's national survey and mapping organisation; it undertakes geodetic control, topographical mapping, national mapping infrastructure and related survey work
options.C: A satellite navigation system developed by India
options.D: A geospatial platform for disaster management

questions.explanation: Survey of India (SoI), under the Department of Science and Technology, is India's national survey and mapping organisation. It undertakes geodetic control, topographical mapping, national mapping infrastructure and related survey work.
questions.source: Cartography and Map Reading, Section 3.8.5 (Indian mapping institutions)

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the National Remote Sensing Centre (NRSC)?

options.A: India's national survey and mapping organisation
options.B: An ISRO centre responsible for acquisition, processing, supply and dissemination of remote-sensing data and related applications, including satellite data reception and geospatial products
options.C: A satellite navigation system developed by India

questions.explanation: NRSC is an ISRO centre responsible for acquisition, processing, supply and dissemination of remote-sensing data and related applications, including satellite data reception and geospatial products.
questions.source: Cartography and Map Reading, Section 3.8.5 (Indian mapping institutions)

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is ISRO's role in Earth observation?

options.A: ISRO develops and operates Earth-observation satellites and applications for agriculture, water resources, land-use planning, forestry, ocean studies, weather-related services, disaster management and national development
options.B: ISRO is responsible only for satellite navigation
options.C: ISRO is responsible only for space exploration beyond Earth
options.D: ISRO is responsible only for telecommunications

questions.explanation: ISRO develops and operates Earth-observation satellites and applications for agriculture, water resources, land-use planning, forestry, ocean studies, weather-related services, disaster management and national development.
questions.source: Cartography and Map Reading, Section 3.8.5 (Indian mapping institutions)

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is Bhuvan?

options.B: ISRO/NRSC's geospatial platform that provides visualisation and access to satellite imagery, thematic maps and geospatial applications
options.C: A meteorological and oceanographic data archive

questions.explanation: Bhuvan is ISRO/NRSC's geospatial platform that provides visualisation and access to satellite imagery, thematic maps and geospatial applications. Available layers and services depend on the portal's current release and access rules.
questions.source: Cartography and Map Reading, Section 3.8.5 (Indian mapping institutions)

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is Bhoonidhi?

options.A: An NRSC/ISRO platform for discovery and access to Indian and selected international Earth-observation satellite data products, subject to data policy and registration or access conditions

questions.explanation: Bhoonidhi is an NRSC/ISRO platform for discovery and access to Indian and selected international Earth-observation satellite data products, subject to data policy and registration or access conditions.
questions.source: Cartography and Map Reading, Section 3.8.5 (Indian mapping institutions)

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is MOSDAC?

options.A: A geospatial platform for visualisation of Earth-observation data
options.B: Meteorological and Oceanographic Satellite Data Archival Centre, an ISRO portal providing satellite-derived meteorological and oceanographic data, products and services

questions.explanation: MOSDAC is the Meteorological and Oceanographic Satellite Data Archival Centre, an ISRO portal providing satellite-derived meteorological and oceanographic data, products and services.
questions.source: Cartography and Map Reading, Section 3.8.5 (Indian mapping institutions)

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is VEDAS?

options.B: Visualisation of Earth Observation Data and Archival System, an ISRO/NRSC geospatial platform for visualisation and analysis of Earth-observation data and thematic applications

questions.explanation: VEDAS is the Visualisation of Earth Observation Data and Archival System, an ISRO/NRSC geospatial platform for visualisation and analysis of Earth-observation data and thematic applications.
questions.source: Cartography and Map Reading, Section 3.8.5 (Indian mapping institutions)

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the National Database for Emergency Management (NDEM)?

options.A: An ISRO/NRSC-supported geospatial database and decision-support initiative intended to provide multi-scale spatial information for disaster management and emergency response
options.D: A platform for accessing satellite data products

questions.explanation: NDEM is an ISRO/NRSC-supported geospatial database and decision-support initiative intended to provide multi-scale spatial information for disaster management and emergency response.
questions.source: Cartography and Map Reading, Section 3.8.5 (Indian mapping institutions)

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is NavIC?

options.A: A geospatial platform for satellite imagery

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: If it is 12:00 noon at Greenwich, what is the local mean solar time at 120°E?
questions.explanation: 120 × 4 = 480 minutes = 8 hours. Since 120°E is east of Greenwich, local time is 12:00 + 8 hours = 20:00 (8:00 p.m.).

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: If it is 12:00 noon at Greenwich, what is the local mean solar time at 60°W?
questions.explanation: 60 × 4 = 240 minutes = 4 hours. Since 60°W is west of Greenwich, local time is 12:00 − 4 hours = 8:00 a.m.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the time difference between 30°E and 75°E?
questions.explanation: Longitude difference = 75° − 30° = 45°. Time difference = 45 × 4 = 180 minutes = 3 hours.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: If it is 10:00 a.m. at 0° longitude, what is the local mean solar time at 45°E?
questions.explanation: 45 × 4 = 180 minutes = 3 hours. Since 45°E is east of Greenwich, local time is 10:00 a.m. + 3 hours = 1:00 p.m.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: If it is 10:00 a.m. at 0° longitude, what is the local mean solar time at 45°W?
questions.explanation: 45 × 4 = 180 minutes = 3 hours. Since 45°W is west of Greenwich, local time is 10:00 a.m. − 3 hours = 7:00 a.m.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: A place is at 120°E. What is its time difference from Indian Standard Time (based on 82°30′E)?
questions.explanation: Longitude difference = 120° − 82°30′ = 37°30′ = 37.5°. Time difference = 37.5 × 4 = 150 minutes = 2 hours 30 minutes. Since 120°E is east of 82°30′E, the place is 2 hours 30 minutes ahead of IST.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: If it is 12:00 noon at Greenwich, what is the local mean solar time at 82°30′E?
questions.explanation: 82.5 × 4 = 330 minutes = 5 hours 30 minutes. Since 82°30′E is east of Greenwich, local time is 12:00 noon + 5 hours 30 minutes = 5:30 p.m.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: If it is 12:00 noon at Greenwich, what is the local mean solar time at 68°7′E?
questions.explanation: 68°7′ ≈ 68.117°. Time difference = 68.117 × 4 = 272.47 minutes ≈ 4 hours 32 minutes. Local time = 12:00 noon + 4 hours 32 minutes = 4:32 p.m. (approximately).

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: If it is 12:00 noon at Greenwich, what is the local mean solar time at 97°25′E?
questions.explanation: 97°25′ ≈ 97.417°. Time difference = 97.417 × 4 = 389.67 minutes ≈ 6 hours 29 minutes. Local time = 12:00 noon + 6 hours 29 minutes = 6:29 p.m. (approximately).

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the time difference between two places if their longitudes differ by 10°?

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: If it is 08:00 at 30°E, what is the local mean solar time at 75°W?
questions.explanation: Longitude difference = 30° + 75° = 105°. Time difference = 105 × 4 = 420 minutes = 7 hours. Since 75°W is west of 30°E, local time is 08:00 − 7 hours = 01:00.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: If it is 22:00 at 120°E, what is the local mean solar time at 30°W?
questions.explanation: Longitude difference = 120° + 30° = 150°. Time difference = 150 × 4 = 600 minutes = 10 hours. Since 30°W is west of 120°E, local time is 22:00 − 10 hours = 12:00.
