questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the back bearing of 200°?
questions.explanation: For a whole-circle bearing of 180° or more, subtract 180°. 200° − 180° = 020°.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the back bearing of 315°?
questions.explanation: For a whole-circle bearing of 180° or more, subtract 180°. 315° − 180° = 135°.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: A bearing of 270° corresponds to which direction?
questions.explanation: In whole-circle notation from north, west = 270°.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: A bearing of 135° corresponds to which direction?
questions.explanation: Southeast is halfway between east (090°) and south (180°), so the bearing is 135°.
questions.source: Cartography and Map Reading, Section 3.8.1 and 3.8.4

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: A bearing of 225° corresponds to which direction?
questions.explanation: Southwest is halfway between south (180°) and west (270°), so the bearing is 225°.
questions.source: Cartography and Map Reading, Section 3.8.1 and 3.8.4

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: A bearing of 315° corresponds to which direction?
questions.explanation: Northwest is halfway between west (270°) and north (360°), so the bearing is 315°.
questions.source: Cartography and Map Reading, Section 3.8.1 and 3.8.4

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: A bearing of 045° corresponds to which direction?
questions.explanation: Northeast is halfway between north (000°) and east (090°), so the bearing is 045°.
questions.source: Cartography and Map Reading, Section 3.8.1 and 3.8.4

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the difference between a passive and an active remote sensor?

options.A: Passive sensors emit their own energy; active sensors detect naturally available energy
options.B: Passive sensors detect naturally available energy; active sensors emit their own energy and measure the return
options.C: Passive sensors work only at night; active sensors work only during the day
options.D: Passive sensors are used only on satellites; active sensors are used only on aircraft

questions.explanation: Passive sensors detect naturally available energy, such as reflected sunlight or emitted thermal radiation. Active sensors emit their own energy and measure the return, as in radar and lidar.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is spatial resolution in remote sensing?

options.A: The number and width of wavelength bands
options.B: The ground detail or pixel size
options.C: The sensitivity to differences in energy
options.D: How frequently a sensor revisits the same area

questions.explanation: Spatial resolution describes ground detail or pixel size.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is spectral resolution in remote sensing?

options.A: The ground detail or pixel size
options.B: The number and width of wavelength bands
options.C: The sensitivity to differences in energy
options.D: How frequently a sensor revisits the same area

questions.explanation: Spectral resolution describes the number and width of wavelength bands.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is radiometric resolution in remote sensing?

options.A: The ground detail or pixel size
options.B: The number and width of wavelength bands
options.C: The sensitivity to differences in energy
options.D: How frequently a sensor revisits the same area

questions.explanation: Radiometric resolution describes sensitivity to differences in energy.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is temporal resolution in remote sensing?

options.A: The ground detail or pixel size
options.B: The number and width of wavelength bands
options.C: The sensitivity to differences in energy
options.D: How frequently a sensor revisits or acquires the same area

questions.explanation: Temporal resolution describes how frequently a sensor revisits or acquires the same area.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are the main data models in GIS?
questions.explanation: The main data models in GIS are raster (grid cells/pixels) and vector (points, lines and polygons).

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following is a common GIS operation?
questions.explanation: Overlay, buffering and spatial query are all common GIS operations, along with network analysis, interpolation, terrain analysis, geocoding, proximity analysis, map algebra and spatial statistics.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the primary function of GPS?

options.A: To store and analyse spatial data
options.B: To determine position, navigation and timing using satellites
options.D: To project the Earth's surface onto a flat map

questions.explanation: GPS is a satellite-based radio-navigation system that provides positioning, navigation and timing services worldwide.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the minimum number of satellites normally required to solve for three-dimensional position and receiver-clock offset in GNSS?
questions.explanation: At least four satellites are normally used to solve for three-dimensional position and receiver-clock offset.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is trilateration in the context of satellite navigation?

options.A: A method of measuring signal travel times from multiple satellites to determine position
options.B: A method of projecting maps onto a flat surface
options.C: A method of classifying satellite imagery
options.D: A method of converting addresses to coordinates

questions.explanation: A receiver measures signal travel times from multiple satellites and uses trilateration with satellite clock and orbit information to determine position.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is digital mapping?

options.A: The creation, storage, analysis and display of maps in digital form, including web maps, mobile maps, navigation maps and GIS-based products
options.B: The scanning of paper maps only
options.C: The use of a compass and paper map
options.D: The printing of maps on a digital printer

questions.explanation: Digital mapping is the creation, storage, analysis and display of maps in digital form, including web maps, mobile maps, navigation maps and GIS-based products.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which projection is a compromise world projection designed for balanced visual appearance?
questions.explanation: Robinson is a compromise world projection designed for balanced visual appearance. It is neither conformal nor equal-area, and several properties are distorted.
questions.source: Cartography and Map Reading, Section 3.8.5 (Projection table)

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which projection preserves distances and directions from the centre correctly?
questions.explanation: Azimuthal equidistant represents distances and directions from the centre correctly. Distortion increases away from the centre; not all pairwise distances are preserved.
questions.source: Cartography and Map Reading, Section 3.8.5 (Projection table)

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which projection is used by UTM zones?
questions.explanation: Transverse Mercator is a conformal cylindrical projection oriented across a central meridian and is used by UTM zones.
questions.source: Cartography and Map Reading, Section 3.8.5 (Projection table)

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: How many longitudinal zones is the UTM grid divided into?
questions.explanation: The UTM grid is divided into 60 longitudinal zones, each 6° wide.
questions.source: Cartography and Map Reading, Section 3.8.5 (Projection table)

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the width of each UTM zone in degrees of longitude?
questions.explanation: Each UTM zone is 6° wide in longitude.
questions.source: Cartography and Map Reading, Section 3.8.5 (Projection table)

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a datum in the context of coordinate systems?

options.A: A reference framework defining the size and shape of Earth and the origin, orientation and scale of a coordinate system
options.B: A line of latitude or longitude
options.D: A unit of distance used on maps

questions.explanation: A datum is a reference framework defining the size and shape of Earth and the origin, orientation and scale of a coordinate system. Coordinates can differ when expressed on different datums.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which global geodetic reference system is widely used and associated with GPS?
questions.explanation: WGS 84 (World Geodetic System 1984) is a widely used global geodetic reference system associated with GPS and many digital mapping applications.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the difference between georeferencing and geocoding?

options.A: Georeferencing assigns real-world coordinates to a map, image or dataset; geocoding converts a textual location description into geographic coordinates
options.B: Georeferencing converts an address into coordinates; geocoding assigns coordinates to a map image
options.C: Both refer to the same process
options.D: Georeferencing is used only for satellite images; geocoding is used only for paper maps

questions.explanation: Georeferencing assigns real-world coordinates to a map, image or dataset so it can be correctly positioned and integrated with other spatial data. Geocoding converts a textual location description, such as an address or place name, into geographic coordinates.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a digital elevation model (DEM) used for?

options.A: Slope, aspect, watershed, visibility, contour and terrain modelling analyses

questions.explanation: DEMs support slope, aspect, watershed, visibility, contour and terrain modelling analyses.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which organisation is responsible for foundational geodetic and topographic mapping in India?
questions.explanation: Survey of India is the national survey and mapping organisation responsible for foundational geodetic and topographic mapping.
questions.source: Cartography and Map Reading, Section 3.8.5 (Indian mapping institutions)

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which organisation is an ISRO centre focused on remote-sensing data reception, processing, dissemination and applications?
questions.explanation: NRSC is an ISRO centre focused on remote-sensing data reception, processing, dissemination and applications.
questions.source: Cartography and Map Reading, Section 3.8.5 (Indian mapping institutions)

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following is an ISRO/NRSC geospatial platform for visualisation and analysis of Earth-observation data?
questions.explanation: VEDAS (Visualisation of Earth Observation Data and Archival System) is an ISRO/NRSC geospatial platform for visualisation and analysis of Earth-observation data and thematic applications.
questions.source: Cartography and Map Reading, Section 3.8.5 (Indian mapping institutions)

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following is an ISRO/NRSC-supported geospatial database and decision-support initiative for disaster management?
questions.explanation: NDEM (National Database for Emergency Management) is an ISRO/NRSC-supported geospatial database and decision-support initiative intended to provide multi-scale spatial information for disaster management and emergency response.
questions.source: Cartography and Map Reading, Section 3.8.5 (Indian mapping institutions)

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following satellite series is used for radar imaging?
questions.explanation: RISAT is used for radar imaging. Resourcesat is for land and resource monitoring; Cartosat for cartographic and high-resolution land imaging; Oceansat for ocean observations.
questions.source: Cartography and Map Reading, Section 3.8.5 (Indian mapping institutions)

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following satellite series is used for ocean observations?
questions.explanation: Oceansat is used for ocean observations.
questions.source: Cartography and Map Reading, Section 3.8.5 (Indian mapping institutions)

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following satellite series is used for cartographic and high-resolution land imaging?
questions.explanation: Cartosat is used for cartographic and high-resolution land imaging.
questions.source: Cartography and Map Reading, Section 3.8.5 (Indian mapping institutions)

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following satellite series is used for land and resource monitoring?
questions.explanation: Resourcesat is used for land and resource monitoring.
questions.source: Cartography and Map Reading, Section 3.8.5 (Indian mapping institutions)

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following provides meteorological and oceanographic satellite data, products and services?
questions.explanation: MOSDAC (Meteorological and Oceanographic Satellite Data Archival Centre) is an ISRO portal providing satellite-derived meteorological and oceanographic data, products and services.
questions.source: Cartography and Map Reading, Section 3.8.5 (Indian mapping institutions)

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following provides discovery and access to Indian and selected international Earth-observation satellite data products?
questions.explanation: Bhoonidhi is an NRSC/ISRO platform for discovery and access to Indian and selected international Earth-observation satellite data products, subject to data policy and registration or access conditions.
questions.source: Cartography and Map Reading, Section 3.8.5 (Indian mapping institutions)

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following provides visualisation and access to satellite imagery, thematic maps and geospatial applications?
questions.explanation: Bhuvan is ISRO/NRSC's geospatial platform that provides visualisation and access to satellite imagery, thematic maps and geospatial applications.
questions.source: Cartography and Map Reading, Section 3.8.5 (Indian mapping institutions)

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following is India's regional satellite navigation system?
questions.explanation: NavIC (Navigation with Indian Constellation) is India's regional satellite navigation system developed by ISRO.
questions.source: Cartography and Map Reading, Section 3.8.5 (Indian mapping institutions)

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following is a global navigation satellite system operated by the United States?
questions.explanation: GPS is the United States-operated global navigation satellite system.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following is a global navigation satellite system operated by Russia?
questions.explanation: GLONASS is Russia's global navigation satellite system.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following is a global navigation satellite system operated by Europe?
questions.explanation: Galileo is Europe's global navigation satellite system.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following is a global navigation satellite system operated by China?
questions.explanation: BeiDou is China's global navigation satellite system.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which type of map is used for land records, property and revenue administration?
questions.explanation: Cadastral maps show individual land parcels, plot boundaries, survey numbers and ownership-related information. They are used for land records, property and revenue administration.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which type of map is used for mineral exploration, engineering geology and earth science?
questions.explanation: Geological maps show rock types, geological structures, faults, folds and age relationships. They are used for mineral exploration, engineering geology and earth science.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which type of map is used for climate study and regional planning?
questions.explanation: Climatic maps show climate elements or classifications such as temperature, rainfall and pressure. They are used for climate study and regional planning.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which type of map is used for historical geography and historical research?
questions.explanation: Historical maps show past political boundaries, routes, events, settlement and territorial change. They are used for historical geography and historical research.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which type of map is used for mapping population, crops, minerals or disease incidence?
questions.explanation: Distribution maps show the spatial occurrence or concentration of a variable, often as a thematic map. They are used for mapping population, crops, minerals or disease incidence.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which type of map is used for global patterns, countries, oceans and world regions?
questions.explanation: A world map is a representation of the whole world, usually using a projection. It is used for global patterns, countries, oceans and world regions.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which type of map is used for surveying, fieldwork, defence, engineering and terrain analysis?
questions.explanation: Topographical maps show detailed natural and human-made features, often with contours, spot heights, roads, streams and settlements. They are used for surveying, fieldwork, defence, engineering and terrain analysis.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which type of map is used for administrative and political reference?
questions.explanation: Political maps show countries, states, districts, boundaries, capitals and settlements. They are used for administrative and political reference.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which type of map is used for physical geography and landform study?
questions.explanation: Physical maps show natural features such as relief, mountains, rivers, plains and lakes. They are used for physical geography and landform study.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which type of map is used for spatial distribution and comparison?
questions.explanation: Thematic maps show one selected theme such as rainfall, population, soil, literacy or crop production. They are used for spatial distribution and comparison.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the significance of the Tropic of Cancer?

options.A: It is the northern limit of overhead Sun during the year and passes through India
options.B: It is the southern limit of overhead Sun during the year
options.C: It is the boundary of the region experiencing at least one 24-hour day or night each year
options.D: It divides the Northern and Southern Hemispheres

questions.explanation: The Tropic of Cancer (approximately 23°26′ N) is the northern limit of overhead Sun during the year and passes through India.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the significance of the Tropic of Capricorn?

options.A: It is the northern limit of overhead Sun during the year
options.B: It is the southern limit of overhead Sun during the year
options.C: It is the boundary of the region experiencing at least one 24-hour day or night each year
options.D: It divides the Eastern and Western Hemispheres

questions.explanation: The Tropic of Capricorn (approximately 23°26′ S) is the southern limit of overhead Sun during the year.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the significance of the Arctic Circle?

options.A: It is the northern limit of overhead Sun during the year
options.B: It is the southern limit of overhead Sun during the year
options.C: It is the boundary of the region experiencing at least one 24-hour day or night each year
options.D: It divides the Eastern and Western Hemispheres

questions.explanation: The Arctic Circle (approximately 66°34′ N) is the boundary of the region experiencing at least one 24-hour day or night each year.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the significance of the Antarctic Circle?

options.A: It is the northern limit of overhead Sun during the year
options.B: It is the southern counterpart of the Arctic Circle
options.C: It divides the Eastern and Western Hemispheres
options.D: It is the largest circle of latitude

questions.explanation: The Antarctic Circle (approximately 66°34′ S) is the southern counterpart of the Arctic Circle.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which is the largest circle of latitude?
questions.explanation: The Equator is the largest circle of latitude. It divides the Northern and Southern Hemispheres.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the difference between grid north and true north?

options.A: Grid north is the direction of the map grid lines; true north is the direction along a meridian toward the geographic North Pole
options.B: Grid north points to the magnetic North Pole; true north points to the grid lines
options.C: Both point to the same direction everywhere
options.D: True north is the direction of the map grid lines; grid north is the direction along a meridian

questions.explanation: Grid north is the direction of the map grid lines. True north is the direction along a meridian toward the geographic North Pole. Grid convergence can create differences between them.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is grid convergence?

options.A: The angle between grid north and true north at a particular location
options.B: The angle between true north and magnetic north
options.C: The difference between local solar time and standard time
options.D: The ratio between map distance and ground distance

questions.explanation: Grid convergence is the angle between grid north and true north at a particular location. Together with magnetic declination, it explains why a compass bearing can differ from a map-grid bearing.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What does a four-figure grid reference identify?

options.A: A 1 km grid square on many standard topographic maps
options.B: A point to about 100 m precision

questions.explanation: A four-figure grid reference identifies a 1 km grid square on many standard topographic maps, using the easting and northing values of the square's southwest corner.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What does a six-figure grid reference identify?

options.B: A point within a grid square, commonly to about 100 m on a 1 km grid

questions.explanation: A six-figure grid reference is a more precise reference locating a point within a grid square, commonly to about 100 m on a 1 km grid.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which rule is followed when giving a grid reference?

options.A: Along the corridor, then up the stairs
options.B: Up the stairs, then along the corridor

questions.explanation: When giving a grid reference, eastings are read before northings, following the rule 'along the corridor, then up the stairs'.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which scale type remains usable after proportional enlargement or reduction of the map, provided the bar is resized with the map?
questions.explanation: A linear or graphic scale is a drawn line or bar divided into labelled ground-distance intervals. It remains usable after proportional enlargement or reduction of the map, provided the bar is resized with the map.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which scale type becomes incorrect if a map is enlarged or reduced without changing the written statement?
questions.explanation: A verbal or statement scale becomes incorrect if a map is enlarged or reduced without changing the written statement. A graphic bar scale changes proportionally with the map.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What does scale factor in a map projection vary with?

options.A: Location and direction in many projections

questions.explanation: Scale factor varies by location and direction in many projections, reflecting projection distortion.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following is an example of an active remote sensing system?
questions.explanation: Active sensors emit their own energy and measure the return, as in radar and lidar.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a passive remote sensing system?
questions.explanation: Passive sensors detect naturally available energy, such as reflected sunlight or emitted thermal radiation.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the purpose of ground truth in remote sensing?

options.A: To verify and calibrate the interpretation of remotely sensed data using field observations or measurements
options.B: To determine the elevation of the ground
options.C: To establish true north on a map
options.D: To create the base map for a GIS

questions.explanation: Ground truth in remote sensing refers to field observations or measurements used to verify and calibrate the interpretation of remotely sensed data.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a common GIS operation?
questions.explanation: Overlay, buffering and spatial query are common GIS operations. Satellite signal transmission is a function of satellite navigation and communication systems, not GIS analysis.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which projection preserves local angles and shapes at sufficiently small scales?
questions.explanation: A conformal projection preserves local angles and shapes at sufficiently small scales, not area or all distances. Mercator is the classic conformal projection.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which projection preserves area relationships but may distort shape, angle and distance?
questions.explanation: An equal-area projection preserves area relationships: regions retain their correct relative areas, although shape, angle and distance may be distorted.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which projection preserves distances from one or more specified points or along selected lines?
questions.explanation: An equidistant projection preserves distances from one or more specified points or along selected lines, depending on the projection. It does not preserve every distance between every pair of points.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What does map generalisation involve?

options.A: Omitting minor features, simplifying lines, combining objects and exaggerating important symbols
options.B: Adding every possible detail to a map
options.C: Converting a paper map to digital form

questions.explanation: Map generalisation is the selective simplification of geographic information to suit a map's scale and purpose. It can involve omitting minor features, simplifying lines, combining objects and exaggerating important symbols.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the primary difference between a map and a plan?

options.A: A plan usually represents a small area at a relatively large scale with considerable detail; a map may cover a much larger area and use greater generalisation
options.B: A map is always digital; a plan is always printed
options.C: A plan shows only natural features; a map shows only human-made features
options.D: A plan is a type of globe; a map is flat

questions.explanation: A plan usually represents a small area at a relatively large scale with considerable detail; a map may cover a much larger area and use greater generalisation. The distinction is conventional rather than absolute.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following is a great circle?
questions.explanation: The Equator is the only great circle among the parallels of latitude.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What do opposite meridians together form?
questions.explanation: A meridian is a semicircle joining the North and South Poles. Opposite meridians together form a great circle.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which statement about the International Date Line is correct?

options.B: It bends around countries and island groups to avoid splitting them
options.C: It is the same as the Prime Meridian
options.D: It is a line of latitude

questions.explanation: The IDL is a conventional line, mostly following 180° longitude through the Pacific, where the calendar date changes by one day when crossed. It bends around countries and island groups to avoid splitting them.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: A place at 45°E has a local time of 14:00. What is the local time at 15°E?
questions.explanation: Longitude difference = 45° − 15° = 30°. Time difference = 30 × 4 = 120 minutes = 2 hours. Since 15°E is west of 45°E, local time is 14:00 − 2 hours = 12:00.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: A place at 30°W has a local time of 09:00. What is the local time at 60°E?
questions.explanation: Longitude difference = 30° + 60° = 90°. Time difference = 90 × 4 = 360 minutes = 6 hours. Since 60°E is east of 30°W, local time is 09:00 + 6 hours = 15:00.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: If it is 06:00 at 0° longitude, what is the local mean solar time at 150°E?
questions.explanation: 150 × 4 = 600 minutes = 10 hours. Since 150°E is east of Greenwich, local time is 06:00 + 10 hours = 16:00.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: If it is 06:00 at 0° longitude, what is the local mean solar time at 150°W?
questions.explanation: 150 × 4 = 600 minutes = 10 hours. Since 150°W is west of Greenwich, local time is 06:00 − 10 hours = 20:00 on the previous day.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: A map has RF 1:20,000. What ground distance does 15 cm represent?

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: On a map, 7.5 cm represents 15 km. What is the RF?

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: A lake is 2.5 km wide. How wide will it appear on a 1:50,000 map?

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: A place has a bearing of 135°. What is its back bearing?
questions.explanation: For a whole-circle bearing less than 180°, add 180°. 135° + 180° = 315°.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: A place has a bearing of 280°. What is its back bearing?
questions.explanation: For a whole-circle bearing of 180° or more, subtract 180°. 280° − 180° = 100°.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: A place has a bearing of 075°. What is its back bearing?
questions.explanation: For a whole-circle bearing less than 180°, add 180°. 075° + 180° = 255°.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the role of colours in map representation?

options.A: Colours are used as symbols and labels to represent real-world features, along with graphic marks, lines and patterns
options.B: Colours are used only for decoration
options.C: Colours have no standard meaning in cartography
options.D: Colours are used only for political boundaries

questions.explanation: A map uses symbols, colours, labels and a defined coordinate reference system. Colours are among the conventional graphic marks used to represent real-world features.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the purpose of a defined coordinate reference system on a map?

options.A: To enable accurate location and integration of spatial data

questions.explanation: A map uses a defined coordinate reference system, which enables accurate location and integration of spatial data.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the range of latitude?
questions.explanation: Latitude ranges from 0° at the Equator to 90°N or 90°S at the poles.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the range of longitude?
questions.explanation: Longitude ranges from 0° to 180°E or 180°W.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What does NRSC stand for?
questions.explanation: NRSC stands for National Remote Sensing Centre, an ISRO centre responsible for remote-sensing data and applications.
questions.source: Cartography and Map Reading, Section 3.8.5 (Indian mapping institutions)

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What does ISRO stand for?
questions.explanation: ISRO stands for Indian Space Research Organisation.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What does NavIC stand for?
questions.explanation: NavIC stands for Navigation with Indian Constellation, India's regional satellite navigation system developed by ISRO.
questions.source: Cartography and Map Reading, Section 3.8.5 (Indian mapping institutions)

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What does MOSDAC stand for?

options.A: Meteorological and Oceanographic Satellite Data Archival Centre
options.C: Marine and Ocean Survey Data Analysis Centre
options.D: Meteorological Observation and Satellite Data Analysis Centre

questions.explanation: MOSDAC stands for Meteorological and Oceanographic Satellite Data Archival Centre, an ISRO portal providing satellite-derived meteorological and oceanographic data, products and services.
questions.source: Cartography and Map Reading, Section 3.8.5 (Indian mapping institutions)

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What does VEDAS stand for?

options.A: Visualisation of Earth Observation Data and Archival System
options.C: Vegetation and Environmental Data Acquisition System

questions.explanation: VEDAS stands for Visualisation of Earth Observation Data and Archival System, an ISRO/NRSC geospatial platform for visualisation and analysis of Earth-observation data and thematic applications.
questions.source: Cartography and Map Reading, Section 3.8.5 (Indian mapping institutions)

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What does NDEM stand for?
questions.explanation: NDEM stands for National Database for Emergency Management, an ISRO/NRSC-supported geospatial database and decision-support initiative for disaster management.
questions.source: Cartography and Map Reading, Section 3.8.5 (Indian mapping institutions)

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What does SoI stand for?
questions.explanation: SoI stands for Survey of India, India's national survey and mapping organisation.
questions.source: Cartography and Map Reading, Section 3.8.5 (Indian mapping institutions)

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What does GNSS stand for?
questions.explanation: GNSS stands for Global Navigation Satellite System, the general term for satellite navigation constellations.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What does GIS stand for?
questions.explanation: GIS stands for Geographic Information System.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What does GPS stand for?
questions.explanation: GPS stands for Global Positioning System, the United States-operated satellite-based radio-navigation system.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What does UTC stand for?
questions.explanation: UTC stands for Coordinated Universal Time, the internationally coordinated time standard based on atomic time.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What does IST stand for?
questions.explanation: IST stands for Indian Standard Time, which is UTC+5:30 and based on the 82°30′E standard meridian.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What does GMT stand for?
questions.explanation: GMT stands for Greenwich Mean Time, originally the mean solar time at the Greenwich meridian.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What does WGS 84 stand for?
questions.explanation: WGS 84 stands for World Geodetic System 1984, a widely used global geodetic reference system.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What does UTM stand for?
questions.explanation: UTM stands for Universal Transverse Mercator, a global projected coordinate system divided into 60 longitudinal zones.
questions.source: Cartography and Map Reading, Section 3.8.5 (Projection table)

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What does DEM stand for?
questions.explanation: DEM stands for Digital Elevation Model, a digital representation of terrain elevation.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What does SAR stand for?
questions.explanation: SAR stands for Synthetic Aperture Radar, an active microwave system that can image through cloud cover and at night.

questions.question: What does IRS stand for in the context of Indian satellites?
questions.explanation: IRS stands for Indian Remote Sensing satellites, India's important Earth-observation satellite series.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: If it is 12:00 noon at Greenwich, what is the local mean solar time at 180°?
questions.explanation: 180 × 4 = 720 minutes = 12 hours. Since 180° is east of Greenwich, local time is 12:00 noon + 12 hours = 00:00 (midnight).

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: If it is 12:00 noon at Greenwich, what is the local mean solar time at 180°W?
questions.explanation: 180 × 4 = 720 minutes = 12 hours. Since 180°W is west of Greenwich, local time is 12:00 noon − 12 hours = 00:00 (midnight).

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the local solar-time difference between India's approximate eastern and western longitudes?
questions.explanation: India spans roughly 68°7′E to 97°25′E, a longitude difference of about 29°18′. At four minutes per degree, the local solar-time difference is approximately 1 hour 57 minutes.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: If it is 12:00 noon at 82°30′E (IST meridian), what is the local mean solar time at 0° longitude?
questions.explanation: 82.5 × 4 = 330 minutes = 5 hours 30 minutes. Since 0° is west of 82°30′E, local time is 12:00 noon − 5 hours 30 minutes = 6:30 a.m.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: A place at 60°E has a local time of 10:00. What is the local time at 30°W?
questions.explanation: Longitude difference = 60° + 30° = 90°. Time difference = 90 × 4 = 360 minutes = 6 hours. Since 30°W is west of 60°E, local time is 10:00 − 6 hours = 04:00.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: A place at 30°W has a local time of 10:00. What is the local time at 60°E?
questions.explanation: Longitude difference = 30° + 60° = 90°. Time difference = 90 × 4 = 360 minutes = 6 hours. Since 60°E is east of 30°W, local time is 10:00 + 6 hours = 16:00.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: If a place is 45° east of another place, what is the time difference between them?
questions.explanation: 45 × 4 = 180 minutes = 3 hours. The place to the east is 3 hours ahead.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: If a place is 75° west of another place, what is the time difference between them?
questions.explanation: 75 × 4 = 300 minutes = 5 hours. The place to the west is 5 hours behind.
